subtype: Approach: test skills without the tool to catch dependence [Revision]
passage:
Pranav stared at the blank page on the verandah step, the cooling tea beside him. His seminar paragraph was due, and without the tool open he could not get past two clumsy lines. It scared him a little: when had that happened?

He told his friend Raghav, who lived in the next lane. Raghav shrugged and said, "Then measure it." They made a plan. Every evening after dinner, one tool-free hour of writing, then, each Sunday, a paragraph on a fresh topic in twenty minutes, with Raghav marking it for clarity out of five.

The first Sunday he scored two. By the fourth, he scored four, and the phrases had begun to come back without prompting.

qa.q: How long was the Sunday paragraph test?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, on a fresh topic.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel when he could not get past two clumsy lines?
qa.a: Pranav felt scared and a little shaken, wondering when he had lost the ability to write on his own.

qa.q: What could Pranav do beside the weekly test to keep improving, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could read good writing and copy out sentences by hand, because noticing how others build sentences trains his own without the tool.

qa.q: How might Raghav see marking Pranav's paragraphs each Sunday?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels like a useful ally, seeing Pranav's score climb from two to four and knowing the blunt remark started it.

grounding: After finding it hard to write unaided, the person schedules tool-free practice and a weekly self-test, revealing overreliance early.
